Ibn al-Mundhir related from him also, regarding ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger﴾: "Jibril."

Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nu'aym in al-Dala'il (Proofs of Prophethood) related from Ibn Mas'ud, regarding ﴿And he certainly saw him at the clear horizon﴾, that he said: "He saw Jibril, who had six hundred wings, which filled the horizon."

al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas regarding the verse, that he said: "It only refers to Jibril, that Muhammad saw him in his form at Sidrat al-Muntaha (the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary)."

Ibn Mardawayh related from him, regarding ﴿at the clear horizon﴾, that he said: "The seventh heaven."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh related through several chains from Ibn Abbas that he used to recite ﴿bi-dhanin﴾ with the letter ḍād, and said: "bi-bakhil" (stingily).

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Mas'ud that he recited "wa ma huwa 'ala al-ghaybi bi-zanin" with the letter ẓā', and said: "He is not accused."

al-Daraqutni in al-Afrad, al-Hakim (who declared it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Khatib in his Tarikh related from Aisha that "the Prophet ﷺ used to recite 'bi-zanin' with the letter ẓā'."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "When He revealed ﴿for whoever among you wills to take a straight path﴾, they said, 'The matter is in our hands: if we wish, we will remain upright, and if we wish, we will not remain upright.' So Jibril descended upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said, 'They have lied, O Muhammad.' ﴿And you will not will except that Allah wills, Lord of the worlds.﴾"

This is a Meccan surah, without any disagreement.

Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "The surah ﴿When the sun is wrapped up﴾ was revealed at Mecca."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from ʿAisha and Ibn al-Zubayr the same.

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim, who graded it sahih, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿUmar that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever would like to look at the Day of Resurrection as if he were seeing it with his own eyes, let him recite: ﴿When the sun is wrapped up﴾, ﴿When the sky is cleft asunder﴾, ﴿When the sky is split open﴾."

In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

His saying: ﴿When the sun is wrapped up﴾. The word "the sun" is in the nominative (raf') by a verb omitted, which is explained by what follows it, through what is called ishtighal (the verb being occupied with an object). This is the view of the Basrans. As for the Kufans and al-Akhfash, it is in the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada').

Al-takwir means gathering together. It is derived from kara al-ʿimamah ʿala raʾsihi, yakuruha (he wraps the turban around his head).

Al-Zajjaj said: It is wrapped up as a turban is wrapped. It is said: "I wrapped the turban on my head, I wrap it (ukawwiruha) with a wrapping (kawran), and I wrapped it with wrapping (takwiran)," when you fold it.

Abu ʿUbayda said: "It is wrapped up like the wrapping of a turban, folded and gathered."

Al-Rabiʿ ibn Khuthaym said: "Kuwwirat" means it was thrown; from this comes "kawwartuhu fa-takawwara," meaning he fell.

Qatadah and al-Kalbi said: its light has gone away.

Mujahid said: it has been obliterated.

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: The sun gathers part of itself to part, then it is folded and thrown.

The conclusion is that takwir either means the folding of its body, or the folding of its light, or throwing it.

﴿And when the stars fall, scattering﴾, that is, they fall down, are dispersed and scatter. It is said: "The bird inkadara from the air" when it swoops down. The original meaning of inkidar is pouring down.

Al-Khalil said: It is said "inkadara ʿalayhim al-qawm" when people come in succession and pour down upon them.

Abu ʿUbayda said: They poured down as a hawk pours down.

Al-Kalbi and ʿAta said: On that day the sky will rain down stars, so no star will remain in the sky without falling to the earth. It was also said that the inkidar of them is the obliteration of their light.

﴿And when the mountains are set in motion﴾, that is, they are uprooted from the earth and set moving in the air. From this is His saying: ﴿And the day We set the mountains in motion, and you see the earth laid bare﴾ [al-Kahf: 47].

﴿And when the pregnant camels are abandoned﴾. Al-ʿisharu (the pregnant she-camels) are the pregnant she-camels in whose bellies are their young; the singular is ʿushrāʾ, and she is the one whose pregnancy has reached ten months; then this remains her name until she gives birth.

He singled out the ʿishar because they are the most precious property among the Arabs and their most valued possession. The meaning of ʿuttilat is: left neglected without a herdsman, because of the great terror they witnessed. It is said that this is by way of metaphor, because on the Day of Resurrection there will be no pregnant she-camel; rather the meaning is that if a man had a pregnant she-camel on that day, or pregnant she-camels, he would abandon them and not turn to them, being occupied with what he is in of the terror of the Day of Resurrection. What will come at the end of the discussion, God willing, indicates that this is in the world.

It is also said that al-ʿishar are the clouds, for the Arabs liken them to the pregnant one; from this is His saying: ﴿And the bearers of burdens﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 2]. Their being abandoned is their not raining. Al-Jumhur read ʿuttilat with doubled tāʾ (tashdid), and Ibn Kathir in one narration from him read it with a single tāʾ (takhfif).

It is also said that the meaning is that dwellings will be left empty, so they will not be inhabited; and it is said that the land whose produce is tithed will be left, so it will not be sown.

﴿And when the wild beasts are gathered﴾. Al-wuhush are what is wild among the land animals. The meaning of ḥushirat is: they are raised up so that some of them retaliate against others, so that the hornless is avenged against the horned.

It is also said that their gathering is their death. It is also said that they, despite their aversion from people today and their scattering in the deserts, will be gathered to people on that day.

Al-Jumhur read ḥushirat with single sīn... [sic: with light (takhfif) ḥāʾ/shīn] and al-Hasan and ʿAmr ibn Maymun read it with doubling (tashdid).

﴿And when the seas are set ablaze﴾, that is, they are kindled so that they become fire blazing.

Al-Farraʾ said: They are filled, by becoming one sea.

It is narrated from Qatadah and Ibn Hibban that the meaning of the verse is: they dry up and not a drop remains in them. It is said: "sajartu al-hawd asjuruhu sajran" when I filled it.

Al-Qushayri said: It is from "sajartu al-tannur asjuruhu sajran," when I heated it.

Ibn Zayd, ʿAtiyyah, Sufyan, Wahb and others said: They are kindled and become fire. It was also said that the meaning of suǧǧirat is that they become red like blood, from the saying "ʿaynun sajraʾ," meaning red-eyed.

Al-Jumhur read suǧǧirat with doubled jīm. Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read it with a single jīm.

﴿And when the souls are paired﴾, that is, the righteous man is joined with the righteous man in Paradise, and the evil man is joined with the evil man in Hell.

ʿAtaʾ said: (p-1590) The souls of the believers are paired with the wide-eyed houris, and the souls of the disbelievers are joined with the devils.

It is also said that every likeness is joined to its likeness in authority, as in His saying: ﴿Gather those who did wrong and their spouses﴾ [al-Saffat: 22]. ʿIkrimah said: ﴿And when the souls are paired﴾ means the spirits are joined to the bodies.

Al-Hasan said: Every person is joined to his group: Jews with Jews, Christians with Christians, Magians with Magians, and everyone who worshipped anything besides Allah is joined to one another, and hypocrites with hypocrites, and believers with believers.

It is also said that the deviant is joined with whoever misled him, a devil or a human, and the obedient is joined with whoever called him to obedience from the prophets and believers.

It is also said that souls are joined with their deeds.

﴿And when the buried infant girl is asked﴾, that is, the girl buried alive. The Arabs, when a daughter was born to one of them, would bury her alive, for fear of shame or poverty. It is said: "wa'ada yaʾidu wa'dan, fa-huwa wā'id," and the one done to is mawʾud. Its root is taken from heaviness, because she is buried, and earth is thrown upon her, which burdens her so she dies. From this is His saying: ﴿and their preserving does not burden Him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255], meaning does not burden Him. From this is the saying of Mutammim ibn Nuwayrah:

A buried girl interred in a cave

And from this is the saying of the rajiz:

I named her when she was born, she would die, and the grave is a relative, a guarantor; I threw her away.

Al-Jumhur read al-mawʾudah with a hamza between two quiescent waws, like al-mawʿudah. Al-Bazzi, in one narration from him, read it with a hamza with damma followed by a quiescent waw.

Al-Aʿmash read "al-mawdah" in the pattern of "al-mawzah."

Al-Jumhur read suʾilat in the passive voice. Al-Hasan read it with kasra on the sīn, from sāla yasīlu.

Al-Jumhur read qutilat with light (takhfif) in the passive voice. Abu Jaʿfar read it with tashdid, for intensification.

ʿAli, Ibn Masʿud and Ibn ʿAbbas read "saʾalat" in the active voice, "qatalt" with damma on the final tāʾ.

The meaning of suʾilat according to the reading of al-Jumhur is that the question is directed to her to show complete anger against her killer, to the point that he does not deserve to be addressed and asked about this, and in it is severe rebuke and reproach for her killer.

Al-Hasan said: Allah intended to rebuke her killer, because she was killed without any sin. In the codex of Ubayy: "And when the buried girl asks: For what sin were I killed?"

﴿And when the pages are spread out﴾, meaning the pages of deeds are spread out for reckoning, because they are folded at death and spread out at the reckoning. Each person stands before his page and knows what is in it, and says: ﴿What is this book that leaves out nothing small or great, but counts it all?﴾ [al-Kahf: 49]. Nafiʿ, ʿAsim, Ibn ʿAmir and Abu ʿAmr read nushirat with light (takhfif). The rest read it with doubling (tashdid), for intensification.

﴿And when the sky is stripped away﴾. Al-kashṭ is tearing off with great adhesion, so the sky is stripped as skin is stripped from a ram. The form with qāf, al-qashṭ, is a dialect variant of al-kashṭ, and it is the reading of Ibn Masʿud.

Al-Zajjaj said: It is uprooted as a roof is pulled off.

Al-Farraʾ said: It is pulled off and then rolled up.

Muqatil said: It is uncovered from what is in it.

Al-Wahidi said: The meaning of kashṭ is lifting something off something that had covered it.

﴿And when Hell is set blazing﴾, that is, it is kindled for the enemies of Allah with an intense kindling.

Al-Jumhur read suʿirat with light (takhfif). Nafiʿ, Ibn Dhakwan and Hafs read it with doubling (tashdid), because it is kindled time after time.

Qatadah said: Its fuel is the anger of Allah and the sins of the children of Adam.

﴿And when Paradise is brought near﴾, that is, it is brought near to the God-fearing and made close to them.

Al-Hasan said: They draw near to it, not that it moves from its place.

Ibn Zayd said: The meaning of uzlifat is: it is adorned.

The first is more preferred, because zulfa in the speech of the Arabs means nearness.

It is said: These twelve matters: six of them are in the world, from the beginning of the surah up to His saying: ﴿And when the seas are set ablaze﴾, and six are in the Hereafter, namely ﴿And when the souls are paired﴾ up to here.

The answer to all of them is His saying: ﴿A soul will know what it has brought forth﴾, on the basis that the intended time is the extended period from this world to the Hereafter. But not in the sense that it knows what it knows at every part of this extended time; rather the meaning is that it knows what it has brought forth at the spreading of the pages, that is, what it did of good or evil. The meaning of "what it has brought forth" is what it brought forth of its deeds, and the intended meaning is the presence of the pages of deeds, or the presence of the deeds themselves, as it is reported that deeds will be shaped into forms that indicate them and by which they are known. The indefinite "soul" (nafs) indicates the establishment of this knowledge for one individual of souls, or for some of them, to indicate that its establishment for all of its individuals is so manifest and clear that it is hidden from no one. This is supported by His saying: ﴿The day every soul will find what it has done of good present﴾ [Al ʿImran: 30]. It was also said that this may be to convey that when any soul knows at that time what it has brought forth, it becomes obligatory upon every soul to correct its deeds, lest it be that same soul which knew what it had brought forth; how much more so when every soul knows it, along the lines of your saying to one whom you advise: "Perhaps you will regret what you did," for a person often regrets his deed.

﴿So I swear by the receding stars﴾. The "lā" is extra, as its verification was previously established, as was the verification of what is said about it at the beginning of Surat al-Qiyamah. That is: "fa-uqsimu bil-khunnas," I swear by the khunnas, which are the stars. They are called khunnas from khanasa, meaning to recede, because they recede by day and become hidden and unseen. They are Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus and Mercury, as the exegetes mentioned.

The reason for singling them out from among all the other stars is that they face the sun and traverse the Milky Way.

Al-Sihah says: The khunnas are all the stars, because they recede when setting, or because they are hidden by day, or it is said they are the wandering stars among them, not the fixed ones.

Al-Farra' said: They are the five stars mentioned, because they recede in their course and hide, as the gazelles hide in caves. It is said they were called khunnas because of their retreat, for they are the perplexed stars that go back and then go straight.

It is said: khanasa ʿanhu yakhnisu khunūsan when he withdrew, and akhnasahu when another made him stay behind and left him. Al-khunnas is the recession of the nose from the face with a slight rise at the tip.

The meaning of al-jawar is that they run along with the sun and the moon. The meaning of al-kunnas is that they return until they are hidden under the light of the sun. So their khunūs is their return, and their kunūs is their hiding under its light. It is said their khunūs is their concealment by day, and their kunūs is their setting.

Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: They are the stars that recede by day and set. The meaning is close, because they fall back in the day from sight due to their faintness, so they are not seen, and they appear at night, and hide at the time of their setting.

It is said the intended meaning is wild cattle, since they are described by khunnas, by jawar, and by kunnas.

ʿIkrimah said: The khunnas are the cows and the kunnas are the gazelles; they recede when they see a person, shrink back, retreat and enter their thicket.

It is said they are the angels.

The first is preferred because of the mention of the night and the morning after this, and al-kunnas is derived from al-kunnas, the thicket in which the wild animal hides. Khunnas is the plural of khanis and khanisah. Kunnas is the plural of kanis and kanisah.

﴿By the night when it sets its darkness﴾. The people of language said: it is one of the opposites; it is said "ʿasʿasa al-layl" when it approached, and "ʿasʿasa" when it withdrew.

The commentary also shows that the meaning intended here is "it turned its back" (adbara), in His saying: ﴿And by the dawn when it breathes﴾. Al-Farra' said: The exegetes agreed that the meaning of ʿasʿasa ("to draw near in darkness" or "to withdraw") is adbara ("it turned its back"). This is how al-Jawhari transmitted it from him. Al-Hasan said: it came forward with its darkness.

Al-Farra' said: The Arabs say ʿasʿasa al-layl ("the night ʿasʿasa") when it approaches, and also when it withdraws. This does not contradict what was reported from him earlier, because he related that the exegetes agreed to interpret the word in this verse as adbara, although in origin the word is shared between approach and withdrawal.

Al-Mubarrad said: It is one of the words with opposite meanings (al-adداد, "al-addad").

He said: Both meanings return to one thing, which is the beginning of darkness at its onset and its withdrawal at its end.

Ru'ba ibn al-Ajjaj said:
"O Hind, how quickly you ta'assasa,
after you had been a youth who grew up (tarʿarʿa)."

And Imru' al-Qays said:
"It ʿasʿasa until, if we wished, when it drew near,
there would have been for us a brand from its fire."

And another said:
"The water over the old campsite ta'assasa."

﴿And by the dawn when it breathes﴾. Tanaffus (breathing) originally means the exit of a breeze from the inside.

The "breathing" of the dawn is its coming, because it comes with a spirit and a breeze, so this was figuratively called its breathing.

Al-Wahidi said: tanaffasa means its light extended until it became day, and from this it is said of the day when it increases: it "breathed."

It was also said: ﴿when it breathes﴾ means when it splits and cleaves open. From this comes tanaffasat al-qaws, meaning the bow cracked.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the answer to the oath, saying: ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger﴾. He means Gabriel, because he descended with it from God, glorified is He, to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The word "word" was attributed to Gabriel because he was sent with it. It was also said that the "messenger" in the verse is Muhammad (ﷺ), but the first is more preferable.

Then He described the said messenger with praiseworthy attributes, saying: ﴿Possessor of power, with the Lord of the Throne, secure﴾. That is, one of strong power in carrying out what he was charged with, as in His saying: ﴿Mighty in strength﴾. The meaning of ﴿with the Lord of the Throne, secure﴾ is that he has lofty rank and a firm standing with God, glorified is He. It is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of makīn ("secure"). Originally it was a description, but when it was placed first it became a state. It is also permissible for it to be an adjective (naʿt) of rasūl. It is said: makana fulān ʿinda fulān makānatan, meaning he became one of rank and standing with him.

Abu Salih said: From his standing with the Lord of the Throne is that he enters seventy veils without permission.

The meaning of ﴿obeyed﴾ is that he is obeyed among the angels, who return to him and obey him. ﴿Trustworthy there﴾. The majority recited thumma with a fatha, on the basis that it is an adverb of place for what is distant, and its governing element is "obeyed" or what follows it. The meaning is: he is obeyed in the heavens, or trustworthy in them, that is, entrusted with the revelation and other things. Hushaym, Abu Ja'far, and Abu Haywa recited it with a damma, on the basis that it is a conjunction (ʿāṭif). The use of it as a conjunction indicates a gap in rank, because what follows it is greater than what precedes it. As for whoever said that the "messenger" means Muhammad (ﷺ), the meaning is: he possesses power to convey the message to the community, is obeyed, whom whoever obeys God obeys, and is trustworthy regarding the revelation.

﴿And your companion is not mad﴾. The address is to the people of Makkah, and by "your companion" is meant the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The meaning is: O people of Makkah, Muhammad is not mad. Mentioning him with the description of companionship indicates that they know his situation, and that he is not in any way what they accuse him of, such as madness or otherwise, and that they invented this against him knowing that he is the most intelligent and most perfect of people. This sentence falls within the answer to the oath. So God, glorified is He, swore that the Qur'an was brought by Gabriel, and that Muhammad (ﷺ) is not as they say, that he is mad, and that he does not bring the Qur'an from his own self.

﴿And he certainly saw him at the clear horizon﴾. The lam is the answer to an omitted oath, meaning: And by God, Muhammad certainly saw Gabriel at the clear horizon, that is, at the rising of the sun from the east, because when the sun rises from this horizon it is clear, since things are seen from its direction. It was also said that "the clear horizon" means the regions and directions of the sky, and from this is the poet's saying:
"We took by the regions of the sky over you,
for us are its moons and the rising stars."

God, glorified is He, said ﴿And he certainly saw him at the clear horizon﴾ even though he had seen him more than once, because he saw him this time in his form, having six hundred wings. Sufyan said: he saw him at the eastern horizon of the sky. Ibn Bahr said: at the western horizon of the sky. Mujahid said: he saw him toward Ajyad, which is the eastern side of Makkah. "Clear" (al-mubīn) is an attribute of "the horizon," as said by al-Rabi'. It was also said to be an attribute of the one who saw, as said by Mujahid. It was also said that the meaning of the verse is: Muhammad saw his Lord, mighty and majestic is He, and this matter has already been discussed in Surat al-Najm.

﴿And he is not stingy with the unseen﴾, that is, Muhammad (ﷺ) regarding the unseen, meaning the news of the heavens and what he was informed of that was hidden knowledge from the people of Makkah. ﴿Stingy﴾ means accused: that is, he is trustworthy in what he conveys from God, glorified is He. It was also said: ﴿stingy﴾ means miserly, that is, he does not withhold the revelation and does not fall short in conveying it. The cause of this difference is the difference among the readers. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and al-Kisa'i recited it as ﹙ẓanīn﹚ with a shaded ẓā', meaning accused. The ẓinna is the accusation. Abu 'Ubayd preferred this reading and said: because they did not withhold, but they denied him.

The rest recited ﴿ḍanīn﴾ with a ḍād, meaning stingy, from "I withheld something (ḍanantu bi-l-shay'), I withhold (adinnu) with a stinginess (ḍann), when I was stingy." Mujahid said: that is, he does not withhold from you what he knows; rather, he teaches creation the speech of God and His rulings. It was also said that the intended meaning is Gabriel: he is not stingy about the unseen. The first is preferable.

﴿And it is not the word of an accursed devil﴾, that is, the Qur'an is not the word of a devil from among the devils who eavesdrop on hearing, who are pelted with meteors. Al-Kalbi said: He says that the Qur'an is not poetry or soothsaying, as the Quraysh said. 'Ata' said: By the devil he means the white devil who used to come to the Prophet (ﷺ) in the form of Gabriel, wanting to tempt him.

Then God, glorified is He, rebuked them and reproached them, saying: ﴿Then where are you going?﴾, that is, where do you turn away from this Qur'an and from obeying it? Thus Qatadah said. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is: which path will you follow that is clearer than this path which I have made clear to you? It is said: "Where are you going?" and "To where are you going?" Al-Farra' related from the Arabs: "I went to Syria (dhahabtu al-Sham), I left for Iraq (kharajtu al-ʿIrāq), I set off for the market (inṭalaqtu al-sūq)," meaning toward them. He said: We heard it in these three words, and he recited for a man of Banu 'Uqayl:
"Hanifa cries out at us when it sees us,
and which land are you going to with the cry?"
He means: To which land are you going? So he omitted "ilā" (to).

﴿It is only a reminder to the worlds﴾, that is, the Qur'an is only an admonition for all creation and a reminder to them.

His saying: ﴿for whoever among you wills to go straight﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "the worlds," with the repetition of the preposition. The object of "willing," "to go straight," means: for whoever among you wills uprightness upon the truth, faith, and obedience.

﴿And you do not will except that God wills, Lord of the worlds﴾, that is, you do not will uprightness except that God wills that will, so God, glorified is He, informed them that the will regarding guidance belongs to Him, and that they cannot achieve that except by God's will and His guidance. Similar to this is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿No soul could believe except by God's permission﴾ [Yunus: 100]; and His saying: ﴿Even if We had sent down to them the angels and the dead had spoken to them and We had gathered everything before them, they would not have believed unless God willed﴾ [al-An'am: 111]; and His saying: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love, but God guides whom He wills﴾ [al-Qasas: 56]. The Qur'anic verses with this meaning are numerous.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿When the sun is wrapped up﴾, he said: it became dark; ﴿and when the stars fall﴾, he said: they changed.

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Daylami related from Abu Maryam that the Prophet (ﷺ) said regarding His saying: ﴿When the sun is wrapped up﴾: it will be wrapped up in Hell; ﴿and when the stars fall﴾: they will fall in Hell. So whoever is worshipped besides God is in Hell, except for 'Isa and his mother, and if they had been pleased to be worshipped, they would have entered it.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Abu al-'Aliyah, who said: Six verses of this surah are in this world, and people look at them, and six are looked at in the Hereafter. ﴿When the sun is wrapped up﴾ up to ﴿and when the seas are set ablaze﴾: these are in this world, and people look at them. ﴿And when the souls are paired﴾ up to ﴿and when Paradise is brought near﴾: these are in the Hereafter.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya in al-Ahwal and Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: Six signs before the Day of Resurrection: while people are in their markets, the light of the sun goes away. While they are like that, the mountains fall upon the surface of the earth, so they shake, tremble, and become intermixed. The jinn flee to the humans and the humans to the jinn, and the beasts, birds, and wild animals become mixed, and they surge against one another.

﴿And when the wild beasts are gathered﴾: he said: they become mixed. ﴿And when the pregnant camels are neglected﴾: he said: their owners abandon them. ﴿And when the seas are set ablaze﴾: he said: the jinn say to the humans: we will bring you the news, so they set out to the sea, and it is fire blazing. While they are like that, the earth splits with one crack down to the seventh earth and up to the seventh heaven. While they are like that, a wind comes to them and kills them.

Al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And when the wild beasts are gathered﴾: the gathering of the beasts is their death, and the gathering of every thing is death, except the jinn and humans, for they will meet on the Day of Resurrection.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Khatib in al-Muttafiq wa al-Muftariq related from him regarding His saying: ﴿And when the wild beasts are gathered﴾: every thing will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection, to the extent that the animals will be gathered.

al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th related from him also regarding His saying: ﴿And when the seas are set ablaze﴾: they will be set ablaze until they become fire.

al-Tabarani related from him regarding ﴿set ablaze﴾: its water mixed with the water of the earth.

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th related from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, regarding His saying: ﴿And when the souls are paired﴾, he said: A righteous man is joined with a righteous man in Paradise, and an evil man is joined with an evil man in Hell. Likewise is the pairing of souls. In another narration: Then he recited: ﴿Gather those who did wrong and their spouses﴾. Ibn Mardawayh related something similar from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

al-Bazzar, al-Hakim in al-Kuna, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: Qays ibn 'Asim al-Tamimi came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: I buried eight daughters of mine in the Jahiliyyah. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to him: Free a slave on behalf of each one. He said: I am a man of camels. He said: Then offer a camel (badanah) on behalf of each one.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿And when Paradise is brought near﴾: he said: it is brought close.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related through several chains from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib regarding His saying: ﴿So I swear by the stars that recede﴾: they are the stars that hide by night and recede by day, so they are not seen.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him regarding His saying: ﴿So I swear by the stars that recede﴾: five stars: Saturn, Mercury, Jupiter, Mars, and Venus, and nothing crosses the Milky Way except them.

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Khatib in Kitab al-Nujum related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding the verse: he said: They are the seven stars: Saturn, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, the Sun, and the Moon. Their receding (khunus) is their return, and their hiding (kunus) is their disappearance during the day.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 81, verses 1–29 (part 3 of 3):

Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ibn Sa'd, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, related through several chains from Ibn Mas'ud, regarding His saying ﴿by the stars that recede, that run and hide﴾, that he said: "They are the wild cows."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "They are the cows that hide themselves in the shade."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from him, who said: "They hide themselves at the roots of trees, concealing themselves in them."

Ibn Jarir also related from him, who said: "They are the gazelles."

Ibn Rahawayh, Abd ibn Humayd, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman (The Branches of Faith) related from Ali ibn Abi Talib, regarding His saying ﴿the stars that recede, that run and hide﴾, that he said: "They are the planets."

[p-1593] Abd ibn Humayd related from Ibn Abbas: "al-Khunnas are the cows; ﴿al-Jawari al-Kunnas﴾ are the gazelles. Do you not see them, when they are in the shade, how they hide with their necks and extend their gaze?"

Abu Ahmad al-Hakim, in al-Kuna (the book of kunyas), related from Abu al-Udays, who said: "We were with Umar ibn al-Khattab when a man came to him and said, 'O Commander of the Believers, what is ﴿al-Jawari al-Kunnas﴾?' Umar struck the man's turban with a short staff he had with him, and it fell from his head. Umar said, 'Are you a Harurī (an early Kharijite sect)? By Him in whose hand is the soul of Umar ibn al-Khattab, if I found you shaven, I would have cleared the lice from your head.'" This report is munkar (rejected), for the Harūriyyah did not exist in the time of Umar, nor was there any mention of them at that time.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related through several chains from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿and by the night when it departs﴾, that he said: "When it turns back." ﴿And by the dawn when it breathes﴾: "When the day appears at the rising of dawn."

al-Tabarani related from him regarding ﴿when it departs﴾: "The approach of its darkness."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from him also, regarding ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger﴾: "Jibril."

Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nu'aym in al-Dala'il (Proofs of Prophethood) related from Ibn Mas'ud, regarding ﴿And he certainly saw him at the clear horizon﴾, that he said: "He saw Jibril, who had six hundred wings, which filled the horizon."

al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas regarding the verse, that he said: "It only refers to Jibril, that Muhammad saw him in his form at Sidrat al-Muntaha (the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary)."

Ibn Mardawayh related from him, regarding ﴿at the clear horizon﴾, that he said: "The seventh heaven."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh related through several chains from Ibn Abbas that he used to recite ﴿bi-dhanin﴾ with the letter ḍād, and said: "bi-bakhil" (stingily).

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Mas'ud that he recited "wa ma huwa 'ala al-ghaybi bi-zanin" with the letter ẓā', and said: "He is not accused."

al-Daraqutni in al-Afrad, al-Hakim (who declared it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Khatib in his Tarikh related from Aisha that "the Prophet ﷺ used to recite 'bi-zanin' with the letter ẓā'."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "When He revealed ﴿for whoever among you wills to take a straight path﴾, they said, 'The matter is in our hands: if we wish, we will remain upright, and if we wish, we will not remain upright.' So Jibril descended upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said, 'They have lied, O Muhammad.' ﴿And you will not will except that Allah wills, Lord of the worlds.﴾"

This is a Meccan surah, without any disagreement.

Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "The surah ﴿When the sun is wrapped up﴾ was revealed at Mecca."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from ʿAisha and Ibn al-Zubayr the same.

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim, who graded it sahih, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿUmar that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever would like to look at the Day of Resurrection as if he were seeing it with his own eyes, let him recite: ﴿When the sun is wrapped up﴾, ﴿When the sky is cleft asunder﴾, ﴿When the sky is split open﴾."

In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

His saying: ﴿When the sun is wrapped up﴾. The word "the sun" is in the nominative (raf') by a verb omitted, which is explained by what follows it, through what is called ishtighal (the verb being occupied with an object). This is the view of the Basrans. As for the Kufans and al-Akhfash, it is in the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada').

Al-takwir means gathering together. It is derived from kara al-ʿimamah ʿala raʾsihi, yakuruha (he wraps the turban around his head).

Al-Zajjaj said: It is wrapped up as a turban is wrapped. It is said: "I wrapped the turban on my head, I wrap it (ukawwiruha) with a wrapping (kawran), and I wrapped it with wrapping (takwiran)," when you fold it.

Abu ʿUbayda said: "It is wrapped up like the wrapping of a turban, folded and gathered."

Al-Rabiʿ ibn Khuthaym said: "Kuwwirat" means it was thrown; from this comes "kawwartuhu fa-takawwara," meaning he fell.

Qatadah and al-Kalbi said: its light has gone away.

Mujahid said: it has been obliterated.

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: The sun gathers part of itself to part, then it is folded and thrown.

The conclusion is that takwir either means the folding of its body, or the folding of its light, or throwing it.

﴿And when the stars fall, scattering﴾, that is, they fall down, are dispersed and scatter. It is said: "The bird inkadara from the air" when it swoops down. The original meaning of inkidar is pouring down.

Al-Khalil said: It is said "inkadara ʿalayhim al-qawm" when people come in succession and pour down upon them.

Abu ʿUbayda said: They poured down as a hawk pours down.

Al-Kalbi and ʿAta said: On that day the sky will rain down stars, so no star will remain in the sky without falling to the earth. It was also said that the inkidar of them is the obliteration of their light.

﴿And when the mountains are set in motion﴾, that is, they are uprooted from the earth and set moving in the air. From this is His saying: ﴿And the day We set the mountains in motion, and you see the earth laid bare﴾ [al-Kahf: 47].

﴿And when the pregnant camels are abandoned﴾. Al-ʿisharu (the pregnant she-camels) are the pregnant she-camels in whose bellies are their young; the singular is ʿushrāʾ, and she is the one whose pregnancy has reached ten months; then this remains her name until she gives birth.

He singled out the ʿishar because they are the most precious property among the Arabs and their most valued possession. The meaning of ʿuttilat is: left neglected without a herdsman, because of the great terror they witnessed. It is said that this is by way of metaphor, because on the Day of Resurrection there will be no pregnant she-camel; rather the meaning is that if a man had a pregnant she-camel on that day, or pregnant she-camels, he would abandon them and not turn to them, being occupied with what he is in of the terror of the Day of Resurrection. What will come at the end of the discussion, God willing, indicates that this is in the world.

It is also said that al-ʿishar are the clouds, for the Arabs liken them to the pregnant one; from this is His saying: ﴿And the bearers of burdens﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 2]. Their being abandoned is their not raining. Al-Jumhur read ʿuttilat with doubled tāʾ (tashdid), and Ibn Kathir in one narration from him read it with a single tāʾ (takhfif).

It is also said that the meaning is that dwellings will be left empty, so they will not be inhabited; and it is said that the land whose produce is tithed will be left, so it will not be sown.

﴿And when the wild beasts are gathered﴾. Al-wuhush are what is wild among the land animals. The meaning of ḥushirat is: they are raised up so that some of them retaliate against others, so that the hornless is avenged against the horned.

It is also said that their gathering is their death. It is also said that they, despite their aversion from people today and their scattering in the deserts, will be gathered to people on that day.

Al-Jumhur read ḥushirat with single sīn... [sic: with light (takhfif) ḥāʾ/shīn] and al-Hasan and ʿAmr ibn Maymun read it with doubling (tashdid).

﴿And when the seas are set ablaze﴾, that is, they are kindled so that they become fire blazing.

Al-Farraʾ said: They are filled, by becoming one sea.

It is narrated from Qatadah and Ibn Hibban that the meaning of the verse is: they dry up and not a drop remains in them. It is said: "sajartu al-hawd asjuruhu sajran" when I filled it.

Al-Qushayri said: It is from "sajartu al-tannur asjuruhu sajran," when I heated it.

Ibn Zayd, ʿAtiyyah, Sufyan, Wahb and others said: They are kindled and become fire. It was also said that the meaning of suǧǧirat is that they become red like blood, from the saying "ʿaynun sajraʾ," meaning red-eyed.

Al-Jumhur read suǧǧirat with doubled jīm. Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read it with a single jīm.

﴿And when the souls are paired﴾, that is, the righteous man is joined with the righteous man in Paradise, and the evil man is joined with the evil man in Hell.

ʿAtaʾ said: (p-1590) The souls of the believers are paired with the wide-eyed houris, and the souls of the disbelievers are joined with the devils.

It is also said that every likeness is joined to its likeness in authority, as in His saying: ﴿Gather those who did wrong and their spouses﴾ [al-Saffat: 22]. ʿIkrimah said: ﴿And when the souls are paired﴾ means the spirits are joined to the bodies.

Al-Hasan said: Every person is joined to his group: Jews with Jews, Christians with Christians, Magians with Magians, and everyone who worshipped anything besides Allah is joined to one another, and hypocrites with hypocrites, and believers with believers.

It is also said that the deviant is joined with whoever misled him, a devil or a human, and the obedient is joined with whoever called him to obedience from the prophets and believers.

It is also said that souls are joined with their deeds.

﴿And when the buried infant girl is asked﴾, that is, the girl buried alive. The Arabs, when a daughter was born to one of them, would bury her alive, for fear of shame or poverty. It is said: "wa'ada yaʾidu wa'dan, fa-huwa wā'id," and the one done to is mawʾud. Its root is taken from heaviness, because she is buried, and earth is thrown upon her, which burdens her so she dies. From this is His saying: ﴿and their preserving does not burden Him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255], meaning does not burden Him. From this is the saying of Mutammim ibn Nuwayrah:

A buried girl interred in a cave

And from this is the saying of the rajiz:

I named her when she was born, she would die, and the grave is a relative, a guarantor; I threw her away.

Al-Jumhur read al-mawʾudah with a hamza between two quiescent waws, like al-mawʿudah. Al-Bazzi, in one narration from him, read it with a hamza with damma followed by a quiescent waw.

Al-Aʿmash read "al-mawdah" in the pattern of "al-mawzah."

Al-Jumhur read suʾilat in the passive voice. Al-Hasan read it with kasra on the sīn, from sāla yasīlu.

Al-Jumhur read qutilat with light (takhfif) in the passive voice. Abu Jaʿfar read it with tashdid, for intensification.

ʿAli, Ibn Masʿud and Ibn ʿAbbas read "saʾalat" in the active voice, "qatalt" with damma on the final tāʾ.

The meaning of suʾilat according to the reading of al-Jumhur is that the question is directed to her to show complete anger against her killer, to the point that he does not deserve to be addressed and asked about this, and in it is severe rebuke and reproach for her killer.

Al-Hasan said: Allah intended to rebuke her killer, because she was killed without any sin. In the codex of Ubayy: "And when the buried girl asks: For what sin were I killed?"

﴿And when the pages are spread out﴾, meaning the pages of deeds are spread out for reckoning, because they are folded at death and spread out at the reckoning. Each person stands before his page and knows what is in it, and says: ﴿What is this book that leaves out nothing small or great, but counts it all?﴾ [al-Kahf: 49]. Nafiʿ, ʿAsim, Ibn ʿAmir and Abu ʿAmr read nushirat with light (takhfif). The rest read it with doubling (tashdid), for intensification.

﴿And when the sky is stripped away﴾. Al-kashṭ is tearing off with great adhesion, so the sky is stripped as skin is stripped from a ram. The form with qāf, al-qashṭ, is a dialect variant of al-kashṭ, and it is the reading of Ibn Masʿud.

Al-Zajjaj said: It is uprooted as a roof is pulled off.

Al-Farraʾ said: It is pulled off and then rolled up.

Muqatil said: It is uncovered from what is in it.

Al-Wahidi said: The meaning of kashṭ is lifting something off something that had covered it.

﴿And when Hell is set blazing﴾, that is, it is kindled for the enemies of Allah with an intense kindling.

Al-Jumhur read suʿirat with light (takhfif). Nafiʿ, Ibn Dhakwan and Hafs read it with doubling (tashdid), because it is kindled time after time.

Qatadah said: Its fuel is the anger of Allah and the sins of the children of Adam.

﴿And when Paradise is brought near﴾, that is, it is brought near to the God-fearing and made close to them.

Al-Hasan said: They draw near to it, not that it moves from its place.

Ibn Zayd said: The meaning of uzlifat is: it is adorned.

The first is more preferred, because zulfa in the speech of the Arabs means nearness.

It is said: These twelve matters: six of them are in the world, from the beginning of the surah up to His saying: ﴿And when the seas are set ablaze﴾, and six are in the Hereafter, namely ﴿And when the souls are paired﴾ up to here.

The answer to all of them is His saying: ﴿A soul will know what it has brought forth﴾, on the basis that the intended time is the extended period from this world to the Hereafter. But not in the sense that it knows what it knows at every part of this extended time; rather the meaning is that it knows what it has brought forth at the spreading of the pages, that is, what it did of good or evil. The meaning of "what it has brought forth" is what it brought forth of its deeds, and the intended meaning is the presence of the pages of deeds, or the presence of the deeds themselves, as it is reported that deeds will be shaped into forms that indicate them and by which they are known. The indefinite "soul" (nafs) indicates the establishment of this knowledge for one individual of souls, or for some of them, to indicate that its establishment for all of its individuals is so manifest and clear that it is hidden from no one. This is supported by His saying: ﴿The day every soul will find what it has done of good present﴾ [Al ʿImran: 30]. It was also said that this may be to convey that when any soul knows at that time what it has brought forth, it becomes obligatory upon every soul to correct its deeds, lest it be that same soul which knew what it had brought forth; how much more so when every soul knows it, along the lines of your saying to one whom you advise: "Perhaps you will regret what you did," for a person often regrets his deed.

﴿So I swear by the receding stars﴾. The "lā" is extra, as its verification was previously established, as was the verification of what is said about it at the beginning of Surat al-Qiyamah. That is: "fa-uqsimu bil-khunnas," I swear by the khunnas, which are the stars. They are called khunnas from khanasa, meaning to recede, because they recede by day and become hidden and unseen. They are Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus and Mercury, as the exegetes mentioned.

The reason for singling them out from among all the other stars is that they face the sun and traverse the Milky Way.

Al-Sihah says: The khunnas are all the stars, because they recede when setting, or because they are hidden by day, or it is said they are the wandering stars among them, not the fixed ones.

Al-Farra' said: They are the five stars mentioned, because they recede in their course and hide, as the gazelles hide in caves. It is said they were called khunnas because of their retreat, for they are the perplexed stars that go back and then go straight.

It is said: khanasa ʿanhu yakhnisu khunūsan when he withdrew, and akhnasahu when another made him stay behind and left him. Al-khunnas is the recession of the nose from the face with a slight rise at the tip.

The meaning of al-jawar is that they run along with the sun and the moon. The meaning of al-kunnas is that they return until they are hidden under the light of the sun. So their khunūs is their return, and their kunūs is their hiding under its light. It is said their khunūs is their concealment by day, and their kunūs is their setting.

Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: They are the stars that recede by day and set. The meaning is close, because they fall back in the day from sight due to their faintness, so they are not seen, and they appear at night, and hide at the time of their setting.

It is said the intended meaning is wild cattle, since they are described by khunnas, by jawar, and by kunnas.

ʿIkrimah said: The khunnas are the cows and the kunnas are the gazelles; they recede when they see a person, shrink back, retreat and enter their thicket.

It is said they are the angels.

The first is preferred because of the mention of the night and the morning after this, and al-kunnas is derived from al-kunnas, the thicket in which the wild animal hides. Khunnas is the plural of khanis and khanisah. Kunnas is the plural of kanis and kanisah.

﴿By the night when it sets its darkness﴾. The people of language said: it is one of the opposites; it is said "ʿasʿasa al-layl" when it approached, and "ʿasʿasa" when it withdrew.

The commentary also shows that the meaning intended here is "it turned its back" (adbara), in His saying: ﴿And by the dawn when it breathes﴾. Al-Farra' said: The exegetes agreed that the meaning of ʿasʿasa ("to draw near in darkness" or "to withdraw") is adbara ("it turned its back"). This is how al-Jawhari transmitted it from him. Al-Hasan said: it came forward with its darkness.

Al-Farra' said: The Arabs say ʿasʿasa al-layl ("the night ʿasʿasa") when it approaches, and also when it withdraws. This does not contradict what was reported from him earlier, because he related that the exegetes agreed to interpret the word in this verse as adbara, although in origin the word is shared between approach and withdrawal.

Al-Mubarrad said: It is one of the words with opposite meanings (al-adداد, "al-addad").

He said: Both meanings return to one thing, which is the beginning of darkness at its onset and its withdrawal at its end.

Ru'ba ibn al-Ajjaj said:
"O Hind, how quickly you ta'assasa,
after you had been a youth who grew up (tarʿarʿa)."

And Imru' al-Qays said:
"It ʿasʿasa until, if we wished, when it drew near,
there would have been for us a brand from its fire."

And another said:
"The water over the old campsite ta'assasa."

﴿And by the dawn when it breathes﴾. Tanaffus (breathing) originally means the exit of a breeze from the inside.

The "breathing" of the dawn is its coming, because it comes with a spirit and a breeze, so this was figuratively called its breathing.

Al-Wahidi said: tanaffasa means its light extended until it became day, and from this it is said of the day when it increases: it "breathed."

It was also said: ﴿when it breathes﴾ means when it splits and cleaves open. From this comes tanaffasat al-qaws, meaning the bow cracked.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the answer to the oath, saying: ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger﴾. He means Gabriel, because he descended with it from God, glorified is He, to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The word "word" was attributed to Gabriel because he was sent with it. It was also said that the "messenger" in the verse is Muhammad (ﷺ), but the first is more preferable.

Then He described the said messenger with praiseworthy attributes, saying: ﴿Possessor of power, with the Lord of the Throne, secure﴾. That is, one of strong power in carrying out what he was charged with, as in His saying: ﴿Mighty in strength﴾. The meaning of ﴿with the Lord of the Throne, secure﴾ is that he has lofty rank and a firm standing with God, glorified is He. It is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of makīn ("secure"). Originally it was a description, but when it was placed first it became a state. It is also permissible for it to be an adjective (naʿt) of rasūl. It is said: makana fulān ʿinda fulān makānatan, meaning he became one of rank and standing with him.

Abu Salih said: From his standing with the Lord of the Throne is that he enters seventy veils without permission.

The meaning of ﴿obeyed﴾ is that he is obeyed among the angels, who return to him and obey him. ﴿Trustworthy there﴾. The majority recited thumma with a fatha, on the basis that it is an adverb of place for what is distant, and its governing element is "obeyed" or what follows it. The meaning is: he is obeyed in the heavens, or trustworthy in them, that is, entrusted with the revelation and other things. Hushaym, Abu Ja'far, and Abu Haywa recited it with a damma, on the basis that it is a conjunction (ʿāṭif). The use of it as a conjunction indicates a gap in rank, because what follows it is greater than what precedes it. As for whoever said that the "messenger" means Muhammad (ﷺ), the meaning is: he possesses power to convey the message to the community, is obeyed, whom whoever obeys God obeys, and is trustworthy regarding the revelation.

﴿And your companion is not mad﴾. The address is to the people of Makkah, and by "your companion" is meant the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The meaning is: O people of Makkah, Muhammad is not mad. Mentioning him with the description of companionship indicates that they know his situation, and that he is not in any way what they accuse him of, such as madness or otherwise, and that they invented this against him knowing that he is the most intelligent and most perfect of people. This sentence falls within the answer to the oath. So God, glorified is He, swore that the Qur'an was brought by Gabriel, and that Muhammad (ﷺ) is not as they say, that he is mad, and that he does not bring the Qur'an from his own self.

﴿And he certainly saw him at the clear horizon﴾. The lam is the answer to an omitted oath, meaning: And by God, Muhammad certainly saw Gabriel at the clear horizon, that is, at the rising of the sun from the east, because when the sun rises from this horizon it is clear, since things are seen from its direction. It was also said that "the clear horizon" means the regions and directions of the sky, and from this is the poet's saying:
"We took by the regions of the sky over you,
for us are its moons and the rising stars."

God, glorified is He, said ﴿And he certainly saw him at the clear horizon﴾ even though he had seen him more than once, because he saw him this time in his form, having six hundred wings. Sufyan said: he saw him at the eastern horizon of the sky. Ibn Bahr said: at the western horizon of the sky. Mujahid said: he saw him toward Ajyad, which is the eastern side of Makkah. "Clear" (al-mubīn) is an attribute of "the horizon," as said by al-Rabi'. It was also said to be an attribute of the one who saw, as said by Mujahid. It was also said that the meaning of the verse is: Muhammad saw his Lord, mighty and majestic is He, and this matter has already been discussed in Surat al-Najm.

﴿And he is not stingy with the unseen﴾, that is, Muhammad (ﷺ) regarding the unseen, meaning the news of the heavens and what he was informed of that was hidden knowledge from the people of Makkah. ﴿Stingy﴾ means accused: that is, he is trustworthy in what he conveys from God, glorified is He. It was also said: ﴿stingy﴾ means miserly, that is, he does not withhold the revelation and does not fall short in conveying it. The cause of this difference is the difference among the readers. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and al-Kisa'i recited it as ﹙ẓanīn﹚ with a shaded ẓā', meaning accused. The ẓinna is the accusation. Abu 'Ubayd preferred this reading and said: because they did not withhold, but they denied him.

The rest recited ﴿ḍanīn﴾ with a ḍād, meaning stingy, from "I withheld something (ḍanantu bi-l-shay'), I withhold (adinnu) with a stinginess (ḍann), when I was stingy." Mujahid said: that is, he does not withhold from you what he knows; rather, he teaches creation the speech of God and His rulings. It was also said that the intended meaning is Gabriel: he is not stingy about the unseen. The first is preferable.

﴿And it is not the word of an accursed devil﴾, that is, the Qur'an is not the word of a devil from among the devils who eavesdrop on hearing, who are pelted with meteors. Al-Kalbi said: He says that the Qur'an is not poetry or soothsaying, as the Quraysh said. 'Ata' said: By the devil he means the white devil who used to come to the Prophet (ﷺ) in the form of Gabriel, wanting to tempt him.

Then God, glorified is He, rebuked them and reproached them, saying: ﴿Then where are you going?﴾, that is, where do you turn away from this Qur'an and from obeying it? Thus Qatadah said. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is: which path will you follow that is clearer than this path which I have made clear to you? It is said: "Where are you going?" and "To where are you going?" Al-Farra' related from the Arabs: "I went to Syria (dhahabtu al-Sham), I left for Iraq (kharajtu al-ʿIrāq), I set off for the market (inṭalaqtu al-sūq)," meaning toward them. He said: We heard it in these three words, and he recited for a man of Banu 'Uqayl:
"Hanifa cries out at us when it sees us,
and which land are you going to with the cry?"
He means: To which land are you going? So he omitted "ilā" (to).

﴿It is only a reminder to the worlds﴾, that is, the Qur'an is only an admonition for all creation and a reminder to them.

His saying: ﴿for whoever among you wills to go straight﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "the worlds," with the repetition of the preposition. The object of "willing," "to go straight," means: for whoever among you wills uprightness upon the truth, faith, and obedience.

﴿And you do not will except that God wills, Lord of the worlds﴾, that is, you do not will uprightness except that God wills that will, so God, glorified is He, informed them that the will regarding guidance belongs to Him, and that they cannot achieve that except by God's will and His guidance. Similar to this is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿No soul could believe except by God's permission﴾ [Yunus: 100]; and His saying: ﴿Even if We had sent down to them the angels and the dead had spoken to them and We had gathered everything before them, they would not have believed unless God willed﴾ [al-An'am: 111]; and His saying: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love, but God guides whom He wills﴾ [al-Qasas: 56]. The Qur'anic verses with this meaning are numerous.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿When the sun is wrapped up﴾, he said: it became dark; ﴿and when the stars fall﴾, he said: they changed.

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Daylami related from Abu Maryam that the Prophet (ﷺ) said regarding His saying: ﴿When the sun is wrapped up﴾: it will be wrapped up in Hell; ﴿and when the stars fall﴾: they will fall in Hell. So whoever is worshipped besides God is in Hell, except for 'Isa and his mother, and if they had been pleased to be worshipped, they would have entered it.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Abu al-'Aliyah, who said: Six verses of this surah are in this world, and people look at them, and six are looked at in the Hereafter. ﴿When the sun is wrapped up﴾ up to ﴿and when the seas are set ablaze﴾: these are in this world, and people look at them. ﴿And when the souls are paired﴾ up to ﴿and when Paradise is brought near﴾: these are in the Hereafter.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya in al-Ahwal and Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: Six signs before the Day of Resurrection: while people are in their markets, the light of the sun goes away. While they are like that, the mountains fall upon the surface of the earth, so they shake, tremble, and become intermixed. The jinn flee to the humans and the humans to the jinn, and the beasts, birds, and wild animals become mixed, and they surge against one another.

﴿And when the wild beasts are gathered﴾: he said: they become mixed. ﴿And when the pregnant camels are neglected﴾: he said: their owners abandon them. ﴿And when the seas are set ablaze﴾: he said: the jinn say to the humans: we will bring you the news, so they set out to the sea, and it is fire blazing. While they are like that, the earth splits with one crack down to the seventh earth and up to the seventh heaven. While they are like that, a wind comes to them and kills them.

Al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And when the wild beasts are gathered﴾: the gathering of the beasts is their death, and the gathering of every thing is death, except the jinn and humans, for they will meet on the Day of Resurrection.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Khatib in al-Muttafiq wa al-Muftariq related from him regarding His saying: ﴿And when the wild beasts are gathered﴾: every thing will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection, to the extent that the animals will be gathered.

al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th related from him also regarding His saying: ﴿And when the seas are set ablaze﴾: they will be set ablaze until they become fire.

al-Tabarani related from him regarding ﴿set ablaze﴾: its water mixed with the water of the earth.

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th related from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, regarding His saying: ﴿And when the souls are paired﴾, he said: A righteous man is joined with a righteous man in Paradise, and an evil man is joined with an evil man in Hell. Likewise is the pairing of souls. In another narration: Then he recited: ﴿Gather those who did wrong and their spouses﴾. Ibn Mardawayh related something similar from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

al-Bazzar, al-Hakim in al-Kuna, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: Qays ibn 'Asim al-Tamimi came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: I buried eight daughters of mine in the Jahiliyyah. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to him: Free a slave on behalf of each one. He said: I am a man of camels. He said: Then offer a camel (badanah) on behalf of each one.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿And when Paradise is brought near﴾: he said: it is brought close.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related through several chains from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib regarding His saying: ﴿So I swear by the stars that recede﴾: they are the stars that hide by night and recede by day, so they are not seen.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him regarding His saying: ﴿So I swear by the stars that recede﴾: five stars: Saturn, Mercury, Jupiter, Mars, and Venus, and nothing crosses the Milky Way except them.

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Khatib in Kitab al-Nujum related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding the verse: he said: They are the seven stars: Saturn, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, the Sun, and the Moon. Their receding (khunus) is their return, and their hiding (kunus) is their disappearance during the day.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 81, verses 1–29 (part 3 of 3):

Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ibn Sa'd, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, related through several chains from Ibn Mas'ud, regarding His saying ﴿by the stars that recede, that run and hide﴾, that he said: "They are the wild cows."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "They are the cows that hide themselves in the shade."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from him, who said: "They hide themselves at the roots of trees, concealing themselves in them."

Ibn Jarir also related from him, who said: "They are the gazelles."

Ibn Rahawayh, Abd ibn Humayd, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman (The Branches of Faith) related from Ali ibn Abi Talib, regarding His saying ﴿the stars that recede, that run and hide﴾, that he said: "They are the planets."

[p-1593] Abd ibn Humayd related from Ibn Abbas: "al-Khunnas are the cows; ﴿al-Jawari al-Kunnas﴾ are the gazelles. Do you not see them, when they are in the shade, how they hide with their necks and extend their gaze?"

Abu Ahmad al-Hakim, in al-Kuna (the book of kunyas), related from Abu al-Udays, who said: "We were with Umar ibn al-Khattab when a man came to him and said, 'O Commander of the Believers, what is ﴿al-Jawari al-Kunnas﴾?' Umar struck the man's turban with a short staff he had with him, and it fell from his head. Umar said, 'Are you a Harurī (an early Kharijite sect)? By Him in whose hand is the soul of Umar ibn al-Khattab, if I found you shaven, I would have cleared the lice from your head.'" This report is munkar (rejected), for the Harūriyyah did not exist in the time of Umar, nor was there any mention of them at that time.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related through several chains from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿and by the night when it departs﴾, that he said: "When it turns back." ﴿And by the dawn when it breathes﴾: "When the day appears at the rising of dawn."

al-Tabarani related from him regarding ﴿when it departs﴾: "The approach of its darkness."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from him also, regarding ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger﴾: "Jibril."

Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nu'aym in al-Dala'il (Proofs of Prophethood) related from Ibn Mas'ud, regarding ﴿And he certainly saw him at the clear horizon﴾, that he said: "He saw Jibril, who had six hundred wings, which filled the horizon."

al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas regarding the verse, that he said: "It only refers to Jibril, that Muhammad saw him in his form at Sidrat al-Muntaha (the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary)."

Ibn Mardawayh related from him, regarding ﴿at the clear horizon﴾, that he said: "The seventh heaven."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh related through several chains from Ibn Abbas that he used to recite ﴿bi-dhanin﴾ with the letter ḍād, and said: "bi-bakhil" (stingily).

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Mas'ud that he recited "wa ma huwa 'ala al-ghaybi bi-zanin" with the letter ẓā', and said: "He is not accused."

al-Daraqutni in al-Afrad, al-Hakim (who declared it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Khatib in his Tarikh related from Aisha that "the Prophet ﷺ used to recite 'bi-zanin' with the letter ẓā'."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "When He revealed ﴿for whoever among you wills to take a straight path﴾, they said, 'The matter is in our hands: if we wish, we will remain upright, and if we wish, we will not remain upright.' So Jibril descended upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said, 'They have lied, O Muhammad.' ﴿And you will not will except that Allah wills, Lord of the worlds.﴾"

This is a Meccan surah, without any disagreement.

Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "The surah ﴿When the sun is wrapped up﴾ was revealed at Mecca."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from ʿAisha and Ibn al-Zubayr the same.

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim, who graded it sahih, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿUmar that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever would like to look at the Day of Resurrection as if he were seeing it with his own eyes, let him recite: ﴿When the sun is wrapped up﴾, ﴿When the sky is cleft asunder﴾, ﴿When the sky is split open﴾."

In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

His saying: ﴿When the sun is wrapped up﴾. The word "the sun" is in the nominative (raf') by a verb omitted, which is explained by what follows it, through what is called ishtighal (the verb being occupied with an object). This is the view of the Basrans. As for the Kufans and al-Akhfash, it is in the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada').

Al-takwir means gathering together. It is derived from kara al-ʿimamah ʿala raʾsihi, yakuruha (he wraps the turban around his head).

Al-Zajjaj said: It is wrapped up as a turban is wrapped. It is said: "I wrapped the turban on my head, I wrap it (ukawwiruha) with a wrapping (kawran), and I wrapped it with wrapping (takwiran)," when you fold it.

Abu ʿUbayda said: "It is wrapped up like the wrapping of a turban, folded and gathered."

Al-Rabiʿ ibn Khuthaym said: "Kuwwirat" means it was thrown; from this comes "kawwartuhu fa-takawwara," meaning he fell.

Qatadah and al-Kalbi said: its light has gone away.

Mujahid said: it has been obliterated.

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: The sun gathers part of itself to part, then it is folded and thrown.

The conclusion is that takwir either means the folding of its body, or the folding of its light, or throwing it.

﴿And when the stars fall, scattering﴾, that is, they fall down, are dispersed and scatter. It is said: "The bird inkadara from the air" when it swoops down. The original meaning of inkidar is pouring down.

Al-Khalil said: It is said "inkadara ʿalayhim al-qawm" when people come in succession and pour down upon them.

Abu ʿUbayda said: They poured down as a hawk pours down.

Al-Kalbi and ʿAta said: On that day the sky will rain down stars, so no star will remain in the sky without falling to the earth. It was also said that the inkidar of them is the obliteration of their light.

﴿And when the mountains are set in motion﴾, that is, they are uprooted from the earth and set moving in the air. From this is His saying: ﴿And the day We set the mountains in motion, and you see the earth laid bare﴾ [al-Kahf: 47].

﴿And when the pregnant camels are abandoned﴾. Al-ʿisharu (the pregnant she-camels) are the pregnant she-camels in whose bellies are their young; the singular is ʿushrāʾ, and she is the one whose pregnancy has reached ten months; then this remains her name until she gives birth.

He singled out the ʿishar because they are the most precious property among the Arabs and their most valued possession. The meaning of ʿuttilat is: left neglected without a herdsman, because of the great terror they witnessed. It is said that this is by way of metaphor, because on the Day of Resurrection there will be no pregnant she-camel; rather the meaning is that if a man had a pregnant she-camel on that day, or pregnant she-camels, he would abandon them and not turn to them, being occupied with what he is in of the terror of the Day of Resurrection. What will come at the end of the discussion, God willing, indicates that this is in the world.

It is also said that al-ʿishar are the clouds, for the Arabs liken them to the pregnant one; from this is His saying: ﴿And the bearers of burdens﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 2]. Their being abandoned is their not raining. Al-Jumhur read ʿuttilat with doubled tāʾ (tashdid), and Ibn Kathir in one narration from him read it with a single tāʾ (takhfif).

It is also said that the meaning is that dwellings will be left empty, so they will not be inhabited; and it is said that the land whose produce is tithed will be left, so it will not be sown.

﴿And when the wild beasts are gathered﴾. Al-wuhush are what is wild among the land animals. The meaning of ḥushirat is: they are raised up so that some of them retaliate against others, so that the hornless is avenged against the horned.

It is also said that their gathering is their death. It is also said that they, despite their aversion from people today and their scattering in the deserts, will be gathered to people on that day.

Al-Jumhur read ḥushirat with single sīn... [sic: with light (takhfif) ḥāʾ/shīn] and al-Hasan and ʿAmr ibn Maymun read it with doubling (tashdid).

﴿And when the seas are set ablaze﴾, that is, they are kindled so that they become fire blazing.

Al-Farraʾ said: They are filled, by becoming one sea.

It is narrated from Qatadah and Ibn Hibban that the meaning of the verse is: they dry up and not a drop remains in them. It is said: "sajartu al-hawd asjuruhu sajran" when I filled it.

Al-Qushayri said: It is from "sajartu al-tannur asjuruhu sajran," when I heated it.

Ibn Zayd, ʿAtiyyah, Sufyan, Wahb and others said: They are kindled and become fire. It was also said that the meaning of suǧǧirat is that they become red like blood, from the saying "ʿaynun sajraʾ," meaning red-eyed.

Al-Jumhur read suǧǧirat with doubled jīm. Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read it with a single jīm.

﴿And when the souls are paired﴾, that is, the righteous man is joined with the righteous man in Paradise, and the evil man is joined with the evil man in Hell.

ʿAtaʾ said: (p-1590) The souls of the believers are paired with the wide-eyed houris, and the souls of the disbelievers are joined with the devils.

It is also said that every likeness is joined to its likeness in authority, as in His saying: ﴿Gather those who did wrong and their spouses﴾ [al-Saffat: 22]. ʿIkrimah said: ﴿And when the souls are paired﴾ means the spirits are joined to the bodies.

Al-Hasan said: Every person is joined to his group: Jews with Jews, Christians with Christians, Magians with Magians, and everyone who worshipped anything besides Allah is joined to one another, and hypocrites with hypocrites, and believers with believers.

It is also said that the deviant is joined with whoever misled him, a devil or a human, and the obedient is joined with whoever called him to obedience from the prophets and believers.

It is also said that souls are joined with their deeds.

﴿And when the buried infant girl is asked﴾, that is, the girl buried alive. The Arabs, when a daughter was born to one of them, would bury her alive, for fear of shame or poverty. It is said: "wa'ada yaʾidu wa'dan, fa-huwa wā'id," and the one done to is mawʾud. Its root is taken from heaviness, because she is buried, and earth is thrown upon her, which burdens her so she dies. From this is His saying: ﴿and their preserving does not burden Him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255], meaning does not burden Him. From this is the saying of Mutammim ibn Nuwayrah:

A buried girl interred in a cave

And from this is the saying of the rajiz:

I named her when she was born, she would die, and the grave is a relative, a guarantor; I threw her away.

Al-Jumhur read al-mawʾudah with a hamza between two quiescent waws, like al-mawʿudah. Al-Bazzi, in one narration from him, read it with a hamza with damma followed by a quiescent waw.

Al-Aʿmash read "al-mawdah" in the pattern of "al-mawzah."

Al-Jumhur read suʾilat in the passive voice. Al-Hasan read it with kasra on the sīn, from sāla yasīlu.

Al-Jumhur read qutilat with light (takhfif) in the passive voice. Abu Jaʿfar read it with tashdid, for intensification.

ʿAli, Ibn Masʿud and Ibn ʿAbbas read "saʾalat" in the active voice, "qatalt" with damma on the final tāʾ.

The meaning of suʾilat according to the reading of al-Jumhur is that the question is directed to her to show complete anger against her killer, to the point that he does not deserve to be addressed and asked about this, and in it is severe rebuke and reproach for her killer.

Al-Hasan said: Allah intended to rebuke her killer, because she was killed without any sin. In the codex of Ubayy: "And when the buried girl asks: For what sin were I killed?"

﴿And when the pages are spread out﴾, meaning the pages of deeds are spread out for reckoning, because they are folded at death and spread out at the reckoning. Each person stands before his page and knows what is in it, and says: ﴿What is this book that leaves out nothing small or great, but counts it all?﴾ [al-Kahf: 49]. Nafiʿ, ʿAsim, Ibn ʿAmir and Abu ʿAmr read nushirat with light (takhfif). The rest read it with doubling (tashdid), for intensification.

﴿And when the sky is stripped away﴾. Al-kashṭ is tearing off with great adhesion, so the sky is stripped as skin is stripped from a ram. The form with qāf, al-qashṭ, is a dialect variant of al-kashṭ, and it is the reading of Ibn Masʿud.

Al-Zajjaj said: It is uprooted as a roof is pulled off.

Al-Farraʾ said: It is pulled off and then rolled up.

Muqatil said: It is uncovered from what is in it.

Al-Wahidi said: The meaning of kashṭ is lifting something off something that had covered it.

﴿And when Hell is set blazing﴾, that is, it is kindled for the enemies of Allah with an intense kindling.

Al-Jumhur read suʿirat with light (takhfif). Nafiʿ, Ibn Dhakwan and Hafs read it with doubling (tashdid), because it is kindled time after time.

Qatadah said: Its fuel is the anger of Allah and the sins of the children of Adam.

﴿And when Paradise is brought near﴾, that is, it is brought near to the God-fearing and made close to them.

Al-Hasan said: They draw near to it, not that it moves from its place.

Ibn Zayd said: The meaning of uzlifat is: it is adorned.

The first is more preferred, because zulfa in the speech of the Arabs means nearness.

It is said: These twelve matters: six of them are in the world, from the beginning of the surah up to His saying: ﴿And when the seas are set ablaze﴾, and six are in the Hereafter, namely ﴿And when the souls are paired﴾ up to here.

The answer to all of them is His saying: ﴿A soul will know what it has brought forth﴾, on the basis that the intended time is the extended period from this world to the Hereafter. But not in the sense that it knows what it knows at every part of this extended time; rather the meaning is that it knows what it has brought forth at the spreading of the pages, that is, what it did of good or evil. The meaning of "what it has brought forth" is what it brought forth of its deeds, and the intended meaning is the presence of the pages of deeds, or the presence of the deeds themselves, as it is reported that deeds will be shaped into forms that indicate them and by which they are known. The indefinite "soul" (nafs) indicates the establishment of this knowledge for one individual of souls, or for some of them, to indicate that its establishment for all of its individuals is so manifest and clear that it is hidden from no one. This is supported by His saying: ﴿The day every soul will find what it has done of good present﴾ [Al ʿImran: 30]. It was also said that this may be to convey that when any soul knows at that time what it has brought forth, it becomes obligatory upon every soul to correct its deeds, lest it be that same soul which knew what it had brought forth; how much more so when every soul knows it, along the lines of your saying to one whom you advise: "Perhaps you will regret what you did," for a person often regrets his deed.

﴿So I swear by the receding stars﴾. The "lā" is extra, as its verification was previously established, as was the verification of what is said about it at the beginning of Surat al-Qiyamah. That is: "fa-uqsimu bil-khunnas," I swear by the khunnas, which are the stars. They are called khunnas from khanasa, meaning to recede, because they recede by day and become hidden and unseen. They are Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus and Mercury, as the exegetes mentioned.

The reason for singling them out from among all the other stars is that they face the sun and traverse the Milky Way.

Al-Sihah says: The khunnas are all the stars, because they recede when setting, or because they are hidden by day, or it is said they are the wandering stars among them, not the fixed ones.

Al-Farra' said: They are the five stars mentioned, because they recede in their course and hide, as the gazelles hide in caves. It is said they were called khunnas because of their retreat, for they are the perplexed stars that go back and then go straight.

It is said: khanasa ʿanhu yakhnisu khunūsan when he withdrew, and akhnasahu when another made him stay behind and left him. Al-khunnas is the recession of the nose from the face with a slight rise at the tip.

The meaning of al-jawar is that they run along with the sun and the moon. The meaning of al-kunnas is that they return until they are hidden under the light of the sun. So their khunūs is their return, and their kunūs is their hiding under its light. It is said their khunūs is their concealment by day, and their kunūs is their setting.

Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: They are the stars that recede by day and set. The meaning is close, because they fall back in the day from sight due to their faintness, so they are not seen, and they appear at night, and hide at the time of their setting.

It is said the intended meaning is wild cattle, since they are described by khunnas, by jawar, and by kunnas.

ʿIkrimah said: The khunnas are the cows and the kunnas are the gazelles; they recede when they see a person, shrink back, retreat and enter their thicket.

It is said they are the angels.
